solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What schoolkids enjoy Romeo and Juliet season?

parts.note: Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet is a play
a season is a time of year

explanation.surface: A school timetable slotting a term of Shakespeare's tragedy into the syllabus.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo and Juliet looks like the set text; it is simply one example of a PLAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Playtime is the break in the school day when children go out to play.

clue.text: Demonstrated rise of tomato-like food

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading bottom to top, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: a ripe tomato is red; reversed to DER

explanation.surface: A report that some tomato-like produce has been shown to be growing in popularity.
explanation.walkthrough: Provender is an old word for food or fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Provender means provisions, food in general, originally animal fodder.

clue.text: Records where bees go following middle of month

indicators.note: takes the central letters of the word that follows
to follow is to come behind, so the bees' home is written after the middle of the month

parts.note: the middle three letters of mARCh, a month
bees go home to the hive

explanation.surface: A note of where the bees went in the middle of the month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Month' has to be a particular month: mARCh supplies its middle three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the noun for a stored collection of documents, with 'Records' read as a noun, not the verb the surface suggests.

clue.text: Make cautious progress in mostly excellent English

indicators.note: most of the word, so the last letter goes

parts.note: tip-top = excellent, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A school report: steady progress in English, with mostly excellent marks.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a school report, so 'Make cautious progress' looks like a teacher's comment rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To tiptoe is to move cautiously and quietly.

clue.text: Queen can appear in Mother's Day celebrated in church

explanation.surface: The Queen turning up at a Mothering Sunday service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mother's Day' reads as one phrase, but Mother's is the wordplay and Day starts the definition. Martinmas is St Martin's feast on 11 November.
explanation.definitionFit: Martinmas, the feast of St Martin, is a day in the church calendar.

clue.text: Brave and fortunate in pursuit of power

explanation.surface: Fortune favouring the brave who go after power.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'fortune favours the brave', so 'fortunate' looks like part of the definition; it is the wordplay, with P for power in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Plucky means having pluck, courage.

clue.text: Couple obese after one's shifted rich dessert

explanation.surface: Two overweight people turning away from a rich pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: PAIR FAT becomes PAR FAIT when the single I moves along; only that one letter changes place.
explanation.definitionFit: A parfait is a rich frozen dessert of cream, eggs and fruit.

clue.text: Upper-class United dinners suffering vandalism will be not covered

indicators.note: the letters are smashed up and rearranged

parts.note: U = United, as in football team names, plus DINNERS

explanation.surface: Posh football fans' dinners wrecked by vandals, with no insurance to pay.
explanation.walkthrough: Two U's come from two different abbreviations: upper-class, and United as in Man U.
explanation.definitionFit: Uninsured means not covered by an insurance policy.

clue.text: Family member coming over, name's Nike, not European at all

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming over turns the letters upside down
every E is removed, not just one

parts.note: NAME'S NIKE with all its E's (European) taken out

explanation.surface: A relative arriving for a visit, name of Nike, with nothing European about them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At all' matters: both E's must go, leaving NAMSNIK, which reads upward as KINSMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A kinsman is a male blood relative.

clue.text: Old Catholic is a malevolent creature

explanation.surface: A sectarian slur calling an elderly Catholic a monster.
explanation.walkthrough: RC for Roman Catholic is a standard abbreviation; 'is' simply links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Orcs are the evil goblin creatures of Tolkien and fantasy fiction.

clue.text: Theatre backing variety in debased production

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, as a car backs up, so the theatre's letters run in reverse

parts.note: a variety is a version of something

explanation.surface: A theatre backing a variety show in a tawdry staging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like a theatre's financial support; it reverses REP.
explanation.definitionFit: A perversion is a corrupted, debased version of something, a twisted production of the original.

clue.text: Like a TV series is copied for broadcasting

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter, so the letters are spread and rearranged

explanation.surface: A TV series being duplicated for transmission.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface stays in television, so 'broadcasting' reads as transmission; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a series is the classic thing told in instalments, and the adjective describes anything structured that way.

clue.text: Impersonate fancy don
Animals always found on delta

parts.note: Delta is D in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Wildlife that is always to be seen on a river delta.
explanation.walkthrough: E'ER is the poetic contraction of ever, a crossword favourite. In an across answer, 'on' puts one piece after another.
explanation.definitionFit: Deer is its own plural, so it can mean animals.

clue.text: Hit soldier raised in position — a complicated procedure

parts.note: a role is a position; the outer word

explanation.surface: A soldier struck and hoisted into place, a messy business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' applies to both the hit and the soldier, not the soldier alone, which is why the setter puts it after both.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, informal: a long-winded, fussy process full of needless steps.

clue.text: Second important bit

explanation.surface: Ranking something as the second most important part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a rank; it is just S.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a small amount, as in a few words of a language picked up on holiday.

clue.text: Unfaithfulness every former queen's shown during trial

indicators.note: something shown during a trial happens within its span, so these letters go inside the word for trial

parts.note: a try is a trial; the outer word
ER = Elizabeth Regina, a former queen; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A royal trial airing every allegation of an old queen's infidelity.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls queens tried for adultery, which fits the definition neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: betrayal of someone who trusted you, being false to them.

clue.text: Attempt to gamble on small new broker?

explanation.surface: A new stockbroker trying to gamble on small stocks.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a go-between is a broker in the sense of intermediary, not a financial trader.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-between brokers deals between two parties.

clue.text: One directing acts of Wagner?

parts.note: the surface suggests a stage director; the setter means someone who announces and runs circus acts
Wagner's four-opera cycle is known as The Ring, so its director would be master of the Ring

explanation.surface: A conductor in charge of Wagner's operas.
explanation.walkthrough: Wagner's great cycle is The Ring, so its master sounds like a conductor; really a ringmaster directs circus acts in the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringmaster introduces and directs the acts in a circus.

clue.text: For instance, a seaweed thrown up some time ago

indicators.note: in a down clue, thrown up reads the letters bottom to top

parts.note: nori is the seaweed wrapped round sushi

explanation.surface: Seaweed washed up on the shore long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrown up' fits seaweed cast up by the sea; it reverses EG A NORI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Age was a prehistoric era, a time long ago.

clue.text: Shooting protester, not male, before end of rally

indicators.note: 'not male' asks for the protester without the letter standing for male
the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: a marcher is a protester; drop M for male

indicators.note: before means ahead of in time, so in a down answer the trimmed protester is written above

explanation.surface: A demonstrator shot before the end of a rally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shooting' reads as violence at the rally; it is the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: shooting as a sport takes many forms, and bow-and-arrow shooting is one.

clue.text: Maiden butting in to make a knight foolish

parts.note: the monarch dubs a knight; the outer word
M = maiden, a cricket over with no runs

explanation.surface: A damsel interrupting a knighting ceremony and making the knight look silly.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored, abbreviated M on scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumb, informally, means stupid or foolish.

clue.text: One university heartlessly sacked

indicators.note: the middle letter of FIRED is taken out

parts.note: sacked = fired, minus its central R

explanation.surface: A university academic callously dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' looks like the start of the wordplay; it is the definition, as in 'made one'.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjectival sense: 'one' as in 'we are one', joined together as a single whole.

clue.text: Mike's after running scout convention

indicators.note: the letters of SCOUT are run into a new order
after means following behind, so the Mike letter is written below the rearranged scout

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Mike chasing after a scout at a scouting jamboree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scout convention' reads as a jamboree, but the phrase splits: scout is anagram fodder and convention the definition. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an accepted practice, the way things are usually done.

clue.text: Second bag containing one jigsaw picture?

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so the bag wraps around the one

parts.note: a sac is a bag; the outer word

explanation.surface: A bag holding a single jigsaw puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: A mosaic is pieced together like a jigsaw, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A mosaic is a picture made of many small fitted pieces.

clue.text: Make familiar account oddly unfamiliar

explanation.surface: A story that makes a stranger known, though told in an odd way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like the odd-letters signal, but the odd letters of unfamiliar give nothing useful; the phrase is simply QUAINT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used transitively: you introduce someone to a subject until they know it.

clue.text: Youngster's inclination to accept benefit

parts.note: an ascent is an upward slope, an incline; the outer word
the dole is unemployment benefit in Britain

explanation.surface: A teenager's tendency to take state handouts.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as a possessive but stands for 'is'. Inclination is a slope here, not a leaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a teenager, someone between childhood and adulthood.

clue.text: Father whipping son in anger

indicators.note: to whip is to snatch away

explanation.surface: A father beating his son in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whipping' paints a beating; it means stealing S away.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, literary in tone: wrath, fury, as in 'drew the ire of the neighbours'.

clue.text: Religious dissent unknown by present society

indicators.note: by means beside, as in 'a house by the sea', so the unknown sits next to the other pieces

parts.note: present = here, as at a roll call

explanation.surface: Religious dissent unrecognised by modern society.
explanation.walkthrough: Mathematicians call unknowns x, y and z, so any of those letters can stand for 'unknown'.
explanation.definitionFit: Heresy is belief at odds with religious orthodoxy.

clue.text: Gosh! Nimrod's playing — one follows instinctively

explanation.surface: Surprise at a performance of Elgar's Nimrod, with one listener joining in automatically.
explanation.walkthrough: Nimrod is a famous Elgar variation, so 'playing' suits a concert. A myrmidon is an unquestioning follower, from Achilles' loyal soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A myrmidon is a follower who obeys orders without question.
